title: Pigmentation Changes of the Skin
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Every pigment disorder in this chapter comes from one of three changes: the number of melanocytes, the amount of melanin those melanocytes make, or the transfer of melanin into keratinocytes. This chapter works through the benign melanocytic tumor (nevocellular nevus) and the autoimmune loss of melanocytes (vitiligo), then uses them as anchors for the lesions boards use as distractors: dysplastic and congenital nevi, melanoma, albinism, tinea versicolor, postinflammatory hypopigmentation, ephelides, lentigines, melasma, and the diffuse darkening of primary adrenal insufficiency. Questions usually give a description, an age, a distribution, and one bedside or microscopic finding, and expect you to name the cellular mechanism behind it.
prerequisites: Layers of the epidermis and the position of the basal layer on the basement membrane (IN-1)
Melanin synthesis from tyrosine by tyrosinase, and melanosome transfer to keratinocytes (IN-3)
Cell cycle control by p16 (CDKN2A), CDK4, and Rb, and the concept of cellular senescence
Receptor tyrosine kinase signaling through RAS, RAF, MEK, and ERK (the MAPK pathway)
CD8 T cell cytotoxicity, IFN-gamma signaling through JAK-STAT, and chemokine recruitment
Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and negative feedback by cortisol (EN-6)

connections.how: Where a pigment cell sits (basal layer, dermal-epidermal junction, or dermis) is what defines each lesion, so the normal layered architecture is the map for all of them.
A nevus is a clonal proliferation that halts itself through oncogene-induced senescence, which makes it the cleanest example of why a driver mutation alone does not make a cancer.
Vitiligo is organ-specific autoimmunity against a single cell type, and it clusters with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes through shared susceptibility loci.
Skin color is a readout of plasma ACTH, so hyperpigmentation separates primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency without any imaging.
Malassezia species alter pigment by inhibiting tyrosinase, which is why a fungal infection appears in a pigment differential at all.
Ultraviolet light drives both the protective melanin response and the mutational load that converts a stable nevus into melanoma.

terms.def: A neural crest derived, dendritic cell resident in the epidermal basal layer that synthesizes melanin inside melanosomes.
One melanocyte together with the roughly 30 to 40 keratinocytes to which it transfers melanosomes.
A melanocyte that has lost its dendrites and grows in rounded clusters called nests rather than singly along the basal layer.
Permanent cell cycle arrest triggered by strong oncogenic signaling, enforced in melanocytes largely by p16.
The normal finding in a benign nevus that cells become smaller, less pigmented, and more spindled the deeper they lie in the dermis.
A flat, circumscribed change in skin color less than about 1 cm across, with no elevation or scale.
Complete absence of melanin in a lesion, giving a milk-white color, as distinct from hypopigmentation, which is partial loss.
The appearance of new lesions of an existing skin disease at sites of trauma to previously normal skin.
A handheld source of long-wave ultraviolet light, about 365 nm, used to compare melanin content and to detect some fungal pigments.
An increase in single melanocytes spaced along the basal layer, without nest formation.
Proopiomelanocortin, the pituitary precursor protein cleaved into ACTH, beta-lipotropin, and melanocyte stimulating hormone peptides.
A Gs-coupled melanocyte receptor that raises cAMP when bound by alpha-MSH or ACTH and shifts synthesis toward brown-black eumelanin.

sections.title: How a nevocellular nevus forms and how nest location classifies it

blocks.text: Melanocytes are neural crest derived cells that settle in the epidermal basal layer during fetal life, where they sit singly, about one for every five to ten basal keratinocytes, and extend dendrites to supply melanosomes to roughly 30 to 40 keratinocytes each. Darker and lighter skin contain about the same number of melanocytes; the difference lies in melanosome size, melanin content, and the eumelanin to pheomelanin ratio. Any lesion that adds melanocytes, removes them, or changes their output will therefore change color without changing the thickness of the epidermis.

A nevocellular nevus (a common mole) is a benign neoplasm of melanocytes. It begins when a single melanocyte acquires an activating mutation in BRAF, most often the V600E substitution, or in NRAS. Both are components of the MAPK cascade, so the mutation leaves RAF and then MEK and ERK signaling switched on without a growth factor, and the cell proliferates clonally. In the process the cells lose their dendrites and round up into discrete nests, which is the architectural signature of a nevus rather than scattered individual cells along the basal layer.
Why the growth stops

Sustained, high-level oncogenic signaling does not only drive division; it also activates a protective arrest program called oncogene-induced senescence. In melanocytes the main effector is p16, the product of CDKN2A, which inhibits CDK4 and CDK6 and so keeps Rb hypophosphorylated and the cell blocked before S phase. Accumulation of p16 is why a mole reaches a few millimeters, stabilizes, and then stays the same for decades even though it carries a bona fide oncogenic mutation. Melanoma requires additional hits that dismantle this brake, characteristically loss of CDKN2A and activation of the TERT promoter to restore telomere maintenance.

blocks.title: Nevogenesis and its self-limiting brake
steps: Single basal melanocyte acquires activating BRAF V600E or NRAS mutation
MAPK signaling (RAF to MEK to ERK) runs without growth factor
Clonal proliferation; cells lose dendrites and form nests
Strong oncogenic signaling induces p16 (CDKN2A)
CDK4 and CDK6 inhibited, Rb stays active, cells arrest
Lesion stabilizes as a small benign nevus
blocks.caption: The same mutation that starts a nevus also triggers the senescence program that stops it, which is why common nevi are stable.

blocks.text: Classification by where the nests sit

Nevus cells begin at the dermal-epidermal junction and migrate into the dermis over years, so the three named types are stages of one process rather than separate diseases. This is why the type correlates with patient age, and why a flat dark macule in a child and a soft dome-shaped papule in a 60 year old can be the same lesion at different points in its life.

blocks.title: Nevus types by nest location
rows: Slightly raised brown papule, often with a flat rim
Dome-shaped or pedunculated, often tan or skin colored
blocks.caption: As nests descend into the dermis the lesion becomes more raised and usually less pigmented.

blocks.text: Within a benign nevus, cells also change predictably with depth, a finding called maturation. Superficial nests are larger, rounder, clearly nested, and well pigmented; deeper cells become smaller, lose pigment, take on a spindled shape, and may resemble neural or fibrous tissue. Maturation reflects progressive exit from the cell cycle as the clone descends. Loss of maturation, meaning cells that remain large, pigmented, and mitotically active deep in the dermis, is a histologic warning sign for melanoma.

blocks.predict: A 5 mm lesion has nests at the junction and in the superficial dermis, and deep dermal cells that are just as large, pigmented, and mitotically active as the superficial ones. What is the concern, and which brake has failed?
blocks.explain: Answer in terms of senescence, not appearance.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraphs on oncogene-induced senescence and on maturation with depth.

sections.title: Separating a benign nevus from melanoma, and the risk carried by congenital nevi

blocks.text: The clinical features that separate a mole from a melanoma are readouts of growth behavior. A benign nevus is one clone that expanded evenly and then arrested, so it is small (usually under 6 mm), symmetric, sharply bordered, a single uniform brown or tan, and unchanged over years. A melanoma contains subclones proliferating at different rates and directions, producing asymmetry, notched or indistinct borders, mixed colors including black, red, white, and blue-gray, a larger diameter, and visible change over weeks to months.

blocks.title: Benign nevus compared with melanoma
rows: Notched or fading into normal skin
Often over 6 mm; early lesions can be smaller
Evolving in size, shape, color, or symptoms
No maturation, deep mitoses, upward single-cell spread
blocks.caption: The ABCDE criteria are the clinical column of this table.

blocks.text: Two refinements matter. The ugly duckling sign uses the patient as their own control: because one person's nevi usually share a growth pattern and a look, the lesion that does not resemble the others deserves attention even if it meets no single ABCDE criterion. A dysplastic nevus occupies the middle ground, with architectural disorder and cytologic atypia at the junction in a lentiginous, bridging pattern of nests; dysplastic nevi mark increased melanoma risk across the whole skin surface rather than being obligate precursors at that site, and in familial atypical mole and melanoma syndrome they accompany germline CDKN2A mutations.
Why depth decides prognosis

Melanoma grows in two phases. In the radial growth phase cells spread laterally within the epidermis and papillary dermis and have not yet acquired metastatic capacity. In the vertical growth phase a subclone grows as an expansile nodule into the reticular dermis, where it meets lymphatics and blood vessels. Depth of invasion measured from the granular layer (Breslow thickness) is therefore the strongest prognostic variable in localized melanoma, with ulceration and mitotic rate adding to it. A broad, flat, long-standing lesion can therefore carry a better prognosis than a small nodule.

blocks.title: Progression from nevus to metastatic melanoma
steps: Activating BRAF or NRAS mutation plus cumulative ultraviolet damage
Loss of the p16 brake (CDKN2A) and TERT promoter activation
Radial growth phase: lateral epidermal spread, no metastatic capacity
Vertical growth phase: nodular invasion of reticular dermis
Access to dermal lymphatics and vessels
Regional nodal then distant metastasis
blocks.caption: Metastatic potential appears with vertical growth, which Breslow thickness measures.

blocks.text: Congenital melanocytic nevi are present at birth or appear within weeks, are usually larger than acquired nevi, and often bear terminal hairs with nests extending deep around adnexa and nerves. Risk tracks with size: small and medium lesions add little lifetime melanoma risk, whereas large or giant lesions, conventionally those projected to exceed about 20 cm in adult diameter, carry clearly increased risk, and melanoma in them may arise in the dermis rather than at the junction, so it is harder to detect early. Large posterior axial lesions with many satellites also raise the possibility of neurocutaneous melanocytosis, which presents neurologically.

blocks.title: Worked example: two changing moles
blocks.text: Patient A, age 8, has a 4 mm flat, evenly dark brown macule on the back, unchanged for two years. Patient B, age 46, has a 9 mm back lesion with one notched edge, a black zone, a gray-white zone, and four months of enlargement. Patient A's lesion is symmetric, uniform, and stable: a clone arrested by oncogene-induced senescence, and at her age nests sit at the junction, so a junctional nevus fits. Patient B is asymmetric in color and outline and meets the border, color, diameter, and evolution criteria; the gray-white zone suggests regression and the black zone a deeper pigmented subclone. The decision rests on the rate and unevenness of growth, not on darkness.

Vitiligo affects roughly 0.5 to 1 percent of people worldwide and is an organ-specific autoimmune disease in which CD8 T cells recognize melanocyte differentiation antigens, including tyrosinase, gp100, MART-1, and TRP-1, and kill the cells that express them. Because melanocytes are eliminated rather than suppressed, the affected skin cannot synthesize any melanin, so the lesions are fully depigmented and milk-white instead of merely pale. Susceptibility is polygenic, with associations at HLA class II, PTPN22, and NLRP1 among others, and oxidative stress in melanocytes is thought to expose antigen and start the process in genetically predisposed people.

The effector loop is driven by interferon gamma. Melanocyte-specific CD8 T cells that reach the skin release IFN-gamma, which signals through JAK1, JAK2, and STAT1 in keratinocytes and induces the chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10. These bind CXCR3 on circulating T cells and recruit more of them to the same site, so each wave of killing attracts the next. This self-reinforcing circuit explains the progressive, patch-by-patch spread of lesions and the persistence of resident memory T cells in clinically stable skin.

blocks.title: The interferon gamma amplification loop in vitiligo
steps: Oxidative stress exposes melanocyte antigens
Melanocyte-specific CD8 T cells enter the skin
T cells release IFN-gamma
Keratinocytes induce CXCL9 and CXCL10 through JAK-STAT
CXCR3 positive T cells are recruited in greater numbers
More melanocytes are killed, exposing further antigen
blocks.caption: A feed-forward loop: killing releases antigen, which recruits more cytotoxic cells to the same patch.

blocks.text: Findings explained by the mechanism

Lesions are sharply demarcated macules and patches, chalk or milk-white, favoring periorificial skin around the mouth and eyes, the dorsal hands and fingers, the genitals, and skin over bony prominences such as elbows and knees, usually in a symmetric generalized pattern. A segmental variant, confined to one area and often stable after an early phase, is thought to reflect a localized or mosaic trigger. Under a Wood lamp, long-wave ultraviolet light is absorbed by melanin in normal skin but reflected by the depigmented patch, so lesions glow bright blue-white with sharply visible margins; this is how borders are defined in lightly pigmented skin where the lesions are easy to miss. The Koebner phenomenon, new patches at sites of friction, cuts, or burns, reflects the recruitment of circulating autoreactive T cells to injured skin, which is also why pressure-bearing sites are commonly involved. A biopsy shows a normal epidermis with melanocytes absent from the basal layer, often with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate at the advancing edge. White hairs within a patch (leukotrichia) indicate destruction of follicular melanocytes.

Because susceptibility is shared across autoimmune diseases, vitiligo clusters with autoimmune thyroid disease, which is the most common association, as well as type 1 diabetes mellitus, pernicious anemia, alopecia areata, and autoimmune adrenal insufficiency; this cluster is the reason a board question about a depigmenting rash often supplies a thyroid-stimulating hormone value or a vitamin B12 level. A halo nevus, a nevus encircled by a depigmented ring, represents the same cytotoxic response directed at nevus cells and may appear in patients with or without generalized vitiligo.

sections.title: The white patch differential: absent melanocytes versus quiet melanocytes

blocks.text: Four conditions account for most white lesions on examinations, and one question separates them: are the melanocytes gone, or are they present but making or transferring less melanin? Only vitiligo removes them. That single distinction predicts the color (true milk-white depigmentation in vitiligo, off-white or tan hypopigmentation in the others), the sharpness of the border, and the degree of accentuation under a Wood lamp, because accentuation depends on how completely melanin is absent from the lesion compared with the surrounding skin.

In oculocutaneous albinism the melanocytes are present in normal numbers and contain melanosomes, but melanin synthesis is defective, most often because of mutations in TYR (tyrosinase, type 1) or in the OCA2 gene product that regulates melanosomal pH and tyrosinase function (type 2). The deficit is generalized and present from birth rather than patchy and acquired, and it involves the eye: foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, iris transillumination, photophobia, reduced visual acuity, and misrouting of retinal fibers at the optic chiasm. Because melanin normally absorbs ultraviolet photons, these patients carry a high lifetime burden of actinic damage and keratinocyte-derived skin cancers. Albinism also appears as one feature of syndromes with defective lysosome-related organelle trafficking, Chediak-Higashi (LYST) and Hermansky-Pudlak, where the accompanying immunodeficiency or platelet storage pool defect gives the diagnosis away.

Tinea versicolor is pigment change caused by infection. The lipophilic yeast Malassezia, as a commensal that overgrows in sebaceous, warm, humid conditions, releases dicarboxylic acids, including azelaic acid, that inhibit tyrosinase in the melanocytes beneath it. The melanocytes remain in place but their output falls, so the macules are hypopigmented rather than depigmented; in some patients the lesions instead appear hyperpigmented, which is why the name says versicolor. The fine, dry, branny scale on the upper trunk, shoulders, and neck, and a potassium hydroxide preparation showing short, curved hyphae with clusters of round yeast cells, settle the diagnosis.

Postinflammatory hypopigmentation follows resolution of an inflammatory dermatosis such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, or lichen planus. Melanocytes survive but melanosome transfer to keratinocytes is impaired and some melanin was lost with the shed epidermis, so the patch is partially pale, poorly demarcated, located exactly where the earlier rash was, and repigments slowly over months. Pityriasis alba, the pale, finely scaling patches on the cheeks of atopic children, is the common pediatric version.

blocks.title: Distinguishing hypopigmented and depigmented lesions
rows: Acquired, patchy, sharply bordered, often symmetric and periorificial
Generalized from birth, with ocular findings
Upper trunk and shoulders; fine branny scale; pale or dark
Short curved hyphae with yeast clusters
At the site of a prior rash; indistinct borders
blocks.caption: Scale with a positive KOH identifies the fungal cause; sharp borders with bright accentuation identify the autoimmune one.

blocks.text: Two congenital look-alikes are worth naming so they are not mistaken for vitiligo. Nevus depigmentosus is a stable, hypopigmented patch present from early life with normal melanocyte numbers and fewer melanosomes transferred, and the hypomelanotic (ash-leaf) macules of tuberous sclerosis are similar lesions that appear with seizures, cardiac rhabdomyoma, or renal angiomyolipoma. Both are congenital and stable, whereas vitiligo is acquired and progressive.

blocks.predict: A 22 year old has pale, slightly scaling macules across the upper back that became obvious after a sunny summer, with faint copper-orange Wood lamp fluorescence and short hyphae with yeast on KOH. Why are the lesions pale rather than milk-white, and why did sun make them conspicuous?
blocks.explain: Account for the enzyme involved and for the surrounding skin.
blocks.check: Compare with the tinea versicolor paragraph and the opening paragraph of this section.

sections.title: Brown macules: melanocyte number versus melanocyte activity

blocks.text: Localized brown lesions divide on the same axis as the white ones. Either the number of melanocytes along the basal layer is increased, or a normal number of melanocytes is making and exporting more melanin. Lesions in the first group persist independently of season; lesions in the second group wax and wane with whatever is stimulating the melanocyte, usually ultraviolet light or sex steroids. None of the four lesions below contains nests, which is what separates them from a junctional nevus.

Ephelides, or freckles, are small tan to brown macules on sun-exposed skin, typically in fair-skinned, red or blonde haired people carrying loss-of-function MC1R variants. Melanocyte number is normal; ultraviolet light increases melanin synthesis and transfer into the overlying basal keratinocytes, so freckles darken within weeks of sun exposure and fade over winter. Lentigo simplex, by contrast, is a true increase in single melanocytes spaced along an elongated basal layer, the lentiginous pattern, with no nests. It can arise at any age on any site, including covered skin and mucosa, and it does not darken with sun because the lesion is a cellular increase rather than a response to light. Multiple lentigines in characteristic sites suggest a syndrome: perioral and buccal lentigines with intestinal hamartomatous polyps in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (germline STK11), or widespread lentigines with cardiac and growth abnormalities in the multiple lentigines form of Noonan syndrome and in Carney complex.

Solar lentigines develop on chronically sun-damaged skin of middle-aged and older adults, classically the face, dorsal forearms, and backs of the hands. Here chronic ultraviolet exposure has produced both an increase in basal melanocytes and increased melanin along elongated rete ridges, so unlike freckles they do not fade in winter, and unlike lentigo simplex their distribution maps onto cumulative sun exposure. Melasma is hormonally driven: symmetric brown patches on the cheeks, forehead, upper lip, and chin appearing in pregnancy or with estrogen-containing contraceptives, with melanocyte number little changed but melanogenesis upregulated by estrogen and progesterone and strongly amplified by ultraviolet light. Pigment may sit in the epidermis, the dermis within melanophages, or both; epidermal melasma accentuates under a Wood lamp while dermal melasma does not.

Fair skin, MC1R variants, childhood onset
Increased, single cells in lentiginous pattern

Caused by chronic sun; does not fade
Older adults, face and dorsal hands
Increased synthesis, epidermal or dermal or both

sections.title: Diffuse hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency

blocks.text: Diffuse darkening of the skin in adrenal failure is a direct consequence of pituitary feedback. Corticotrophs synthesize proopiomelanocortin (POMC), a precursor cleaved by prohormone convertase 1 into ACTH, beta-lipotropin, and an N-terminal fragment; beta-lipotropin yields beta-endorphin, and in some tissues further cleavage yields alpha and beta melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH). Critically, the first 13 amino acids of ACTH are the alpha-MSH sequence, so ACTH itself is a melanocortin agonist. When the adrenal cortex is destroyed, cortisol falls, negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is removed, CRH and POMC transcription rise, and ACTH concentrations climb severalfold.

ACTH and the MSH peptides bind melanocortin 1 receptor on melanocytes. MC1R is Gs-coupled, so occupancy raises adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP, activates protein kinase A, phosphorylates CREB, and increases transcription of MITF, the master melanocyte transcription factor that drives tyrosinase and other melanogenic enzymes. The result is a shift toward brown-black eumelanin and more melanosome transfer to keratinocytes across the entire skin surface, which is why the pigmentation is generalized rather than patchy.

blocks.caption: Skin color here is a bioassay for plasma ACTH, which is why the distribution of darkening is diagnostic.

blocks.text: The accentuated sites follow regions where melanocytes are already most responsive or where friction and light add stimulus: palmar and other flexural creases, the gingival and buccal mucosa, the areolae, pressure points such as knuckles, elbows, and knees, scars that formed after the onset of disease, and sun-exposed areas. Pigmentation of a scar is useful because it dates the process. In secondary adrenal insufficiency the lesion is pituitary or hypothalamic, so ACTH is low rather than high, no melanocortin drive reaches the skin, and these patients are pale rather than dark; they also retain mineralocorticoid production because aldosterone is regulated chiefly by the renin-angiotensin system and potassium, which is why hyperkalemia and salt craving belong to the primary form.

blocks.title: Causes of diffuse darkening and how to tell them apart

Pale skin; normal potassium; low cortisol with low ACTH
Ectopic ACTH syndrome (for example small cell lung carcinoma)
Hyperpigmentation with cortisol excess, hypokalemic alkalosis, rapid onset
Dermal iron deposition plus increased melanin
Bronze or slate-gray color with diabetes, arthropathy, cirrhosis, high ferritin and transferrin saturation
Insulin and IGF-1 drive keratinocyte and fibroblast growth

integration.text: This chapter is a single mechanism applied repeatedly: pigment reflects melanocyte number, melanocyte output, and melanosome transfer, and each disease changes one of the three. Pathology supplies the clonal logic, since a nevus demonstrates that an activating BRAF or NRAS mutation plus an intact senescence program yields a stable benign tumor, while loss of CDKN2A and TERT activation yield melanoma; the same p16 and Rb circuit taught in general neoplasia appears here at a size a patient can see. Immunology supplies vitiligo, where antigen-specific CD8 killing plus an IFN-gamma, JAK-STAT, CXCL10 recruitment loop explains both progression and the clustering with thyroid autoimmunity and type 1 diabetes. Endocrinology supplies the melanocortin axis, where skin color becomes a readout of plasma ACTH and therefore separates primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency. Microbiology supplies Malassezia, which changes pigment not by killing cells but by inhibiting their key enzyme.

The limits are worth stating. Clinical criteria are probabilistic: ABCDE criteria are sensitive for larger melanomas but miss small nodular and amelanotic lesions, so histology with Breslow thickness remains the reference standard. Wood lamp examination compares melanin content and does not identify a cause; it cannot distinguish vitiligo from a congenital hypomelanotic macule, and dermal pigment such as dermal melasma does not accentuate at all. Two pigment disorders frequently coexist, since autoimmune adrenal insufficiency and vitiligo belong to the same polyglandular cluster, which is why a patient can present with depigmented patches on diffusely darkened skin, a combination that makes sense only when the mechanisms are kept separate.

summary: Melanocyte number is roughly equal across skin tones; color differences come from melanosome size, melanin content, and the eumelanin to pheomelanin ratio.
A nevocellular nevus starts with activating BRAF V600E or NRAS and stops through oncogene-induced senescence enforced by p16, which is why common nevi are small and stable.

Nevi are classified by nest location and move with age: junctional in children, compound in young adults, intradermal in older adults, with cells maturing (smaller, less pigmented, spindled) as they go deeper.
Benign nevi are symmetric, uniform, sharply bordered, and stable; melanoma shows asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm, and evolution, and loses maturation with depth.

Metastatic potential appears in the vertical growth phase, so Breslow thickness is the strongest prognostic measure in localized melanoma; large congenital nevi carry increased risk, small ones little.

Vitiligo is CD8 T cell destruction of melanocytes amplified by IFN-gamma, JAK-STAT, and CXCL10: milk-white sharply bordered macules, bright Wood lamp accentuation, Koebner phenomenon, and melanocytes absent on biopsy.

In vitiligo melanocytes are gone; in albinism, tinea versicolor, and postinflammatory hypopigmentation they are present but make or transfer less melanin, and scale with a positive KOH identifies the fungal cause.
Ephelides have normal melanocyte numbers and darken with sun; lentigines have increased basal melanocytes and persist; melasma reflects estrogen-driven melanogenesis amplified by ultraviolet light.

High ACTH in primary adrenal insufficiency activates MC1R through its alpha-MSH sequence, raising cAMP, MITF, and tyrosinase, which darkens creases, mucosa, and scars; secondary insufficiency has low ACTH and pale skin.
Vitiligo and autoimmune adrenal insufficiency belong to the same polyglandular cluster, so depigmented patches on diffusely darkened skin is a coherent presentation.

verify: Lifetime melanoma risk in large congenital melanocytic nevi is quoted from about 2% to 5% in different sources, and the size threshold for a large or giant lesion is given as projected adult diameter over about 20 cm (sometimes stated as over 40 cm or as a percentage of body surface area). No single figure is stated here as fact.

The ratio of melanocytes to basal keratinocytes is quoted from about 1 in 4 to 1 in 10 depending on body site and source, and the number of keratinocytes per epidermal melanin unit from about 30 to 40.
Reported prevalence of vitiligo ranges from about 0.5% to 2% depending on population and case definition; about 0.5% to 1% is given here as the commonly cited range.
Wood lamp fluorescence in tinea versicolor is present in only a minority of patients and is described variously as yellow-green, copper-orange, or golden; a negative Wood lamp does not exclude it.

Whether ACTH, alpha-MSH, or both are the dominant MC1R ligand in human Addisonian hyperpigmentation is not fully settled; ACTH is presented here as the main driver because its plasma concentration is markedly elevated and it contains the alpha-MSH sequence. Confirm the level of mechanistic detail NABNE expects.

Whether NABNE tests dysplastic nevi, the ugly duckling sign, Breslow thickness, neurocutaneous melanocytosis, and the lentigines syndromes (Peutz-Jeghers, Carney complex, Noonan with multiple lentigines) under this unit, or reserves them for the melanoma and congenital units (IN-13-F, IN-2), should be confirmed against current official materials.
The D in ABCDE is given here as diameter over 6 mm; some sources use D for diameter and others for a changing or elevated lesion. Confirm the wording expected.
